claim: Coronary heart disease (CHD) is one of the most pressing health problems of our time and a major cause of preventable death.
source: Coronary heart disease (CHD) is one of the most pressing health problems of our time and a major cause of preventable death.
evidence: This is a general statement about CHD that draws from established scientific consensus about the public health burden of CHD.

claim: CHD results from complex interactions between genetic and environmental factors.
source: CHD results from complex interactions between genetic and environmental factors.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific knowledge about the multifactorial etiology of CHD.

claim: The CoLaus|PsyCoLaus study is a longitudinal, population-based cohort with baseline assessments from 2003 through 2008 and follow-up visits every 5 years.
source: Study participants are enrolled in the CoLaus|PsyCoLaus study, a longitudinal, population-based cohort with baseline assessments from 2003 through 2008 and follow-up visits every 5 years.
evidence: This describes the study design and timing, which is factual information about the study itself.

claim: 3459 individuals with available genome-wide genotyping data and immunoglobulin G levels for 22 persistent or frequently recurring pathogens were analyzed.
source: We analyzed a subgroup of 3459 individuals with available genome-wide genotyping data and immunoglobulin G levels for 22 persistent or frequently recurring pathogens.
evidence: This describes the sample size and data types available for the analysis.

claim: 210 out of 3459 study participants (6.07%) had at least one CHD event during the 12 years of follow-up.
source: Of the 3459 study participants, 210 (6.07%) had at least one CHD event during the 12 years of follow-up.
evidence: This is a direct report of the observed CHD incidence in the study cohort.

claim: High polygenic risk is independently associated with incident CHD with a hazard ratio of 1.31 (95% CI 1.10–1.56, p=2.64 × 10−3).
source: Multivariable stepwise Cox regression analysis, adjusted for known cardiovascular risk factors, socioeconomic status, and statin intake, revealed that high polygenic risk (hazard ratio [HR] 1.31, 95% CI 1.10–1.56, p=2.64 × 10−3) and infection with Fusobacterium nucleatum (HR 1.63, 95% CI 1.08–2.45, p=1.99 × 10−2) were independently associated with incident CHD.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the multivariable Cox regression analysis performed in the study.

claim: Infection with Fusobacterium nucleatum is independently associated with incident CHD with a hazard ratio of 1.63 (95% CI 1.08–2.45, p=1.99 × 10−2).
source: Multivariable stepwise Cox regression analysis, adjusted for known cardiovascular risk factors, socioeconomic status, and statin intake, revealed that high polygenic risk (hazard ratio [HR] 1.31, 95% CI 1.10–1.56, p=2.64 × 10−3) and infection with Fusobacterium nucleatum (HR 1.63, 95% CI 1.08–2.45, p=1.99 × 10−2) were independently associated with incident CHD.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the multivariable Cox regression analysis performed in the study.

claim: An estimated 17.9 million people die from CVD each year, accounting for 32% of all deaths.
source: An estimated 17.9 million people die from CVD each year, accounting for 32% of all deaths.
evidence: This statement is supported by the citation to Roth et al., 2018 in the preceding sentence.

claim: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the leading cause of mortality worldwide.
source: Worldwide, cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the leading cause of mortality (Roth et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is directly supported by the citation to Roth et al., 2018.

claim: CHD is the most common type of heart disease.
source: CHD is the most common type of heart disease (Roth et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is directly supported by the citation to Roth et al., 2018.

claim: CHD is caused by atherosclerosis, a build-up of plaque inside the walls of the arteries that supply blood to the heart.
source: It is caused by atherosclerosis, a build-up of plaque inside the walls of the arteries that supply blood to the heart.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about the pathophysiology of CHD.

claim: CHD progresses over a long period of time and eventually evolves into symptoms such as chest pain (angina), tightness in the chest, breathing difficulties, and pain in the arms or shoulders.
source: CHD progresses over a long period of time and eventually evolves into symptoms such as chest pain (angina), tightness in the chest, breathing difficulties, and pain in the arms or shoulders (Ambrose and Singh, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by the citation to Ambrose and Singh, 2015.

claim: A complete blockage can cause a heart attack.
source: A complete blockage can cause a heart attack.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about the consequences of complete arterial blockage in CHD.

claim: A combination of demographic, environmental, and genetic factors contribute to the development of CHD.
source: A combination of demographic, environmental, and genetic factors contribute to the development of CHD (Khot et al., 2003; Mendis et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Khot et al., 2003 and Mendis et al., 2011.

claim: The main risk factors associated with the development of CHD are smoking, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and hypertension.
source: The main risk factors associated with the development of CHD – smoking, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and hypertension – have been established by extensive epidemiological research (MacMahon et al., 1990; Stamler et al., 1993; Verschuren et al., 1995; Weintraub, 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to epidemiological research.

claim: Age is an important risk factor for CHD.
source: Age is also an important risk factor for CHD (Castelli, 1984).
evidence: This statement is supported by the citation to Castelli, 1984.

claim: The incidence of CHD is greater in males than in females.
source: Finally, the incidence of CHD is greater in males than in females (Castelli, 1984).
evidence: This statement is supported by the citation to Castelli, 1984.

claim: SCORE2 was developed to predict the 10-year risk of first-onset CVD in European populations.
source: Very recently, a new algorithm, named Systematic COronary Risk Evaluation 2 (SCORE2), was developed to predict the 10-year risk of first-onset CVD in European populations (SCORE2 working group and ESC Cardiovascular risk collaboration, 2021; SCORE2-OP working group and ESC Cardiovascular risk collaboration, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to the SCORE2 working group publications.

claim: SCORE2 has replaced the existing HeartScore scoring system.
source: This score has replaced the existing HeartScore scoring system, and incorporates most of the risk factors mentioned above (Conroy et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by the citation to Conroy et al., 2003 and the preceding SCORE2 citations.

claim: The first familial risk model for CHD was described in 1938.
source: In 1938, the first familial risk model for CHD was described and later confirmed by clinical observations and large studies of twins and of longitudinal cohorts (Müller, 1938; Marenberg et al., 1994; Samani et al., 2007; Abraham et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by the citation to Müller, 1938.

claim: The heritability of CHD has been estimated at 40–60%, even after controlling for known risk factors.
source: Based on whole-genome approaches, the heritability of CHD has been estimated at 40–60%, even after controlling for known risk factors (Vinkhuyzen et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by the citation to Vinkhuyzen et al., 2013.

claim: Multiple clinical studies have identified inflammatory risk factors that are predictive of future cardiovascular events.
source: Multiple clinical studies have identified inflammatory risk factors that are predictive of future cardiovascular events (Alfaddagh et al., 2020; Libby, 2006; Hansson, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple clinical studies.

claim: Endothelial dysfunction and subintimal cholesterol trigger an inflammatory cascade, involving activated macrophages and leading to atherosclerotic lesions.
source: Endothelial dysfunction and subintimal cholesterol have been shown to trigger an inflammatory cascade, involving activated macrophages and leading to atherosclerotic lesions.
evidence: This statement describes established mechanisms of atherosclerosis development, drawing from scientific knowledge.

claim: Inflammasome formation in macrophages plays an essential role in the propagation of inflammation through production of interleukin (IL)-1β.
source: At the molecular level, inflammasome formation in macrophages plays, through their production of interleukin (IL)-1β, an essential role in the propagation of inflammation.
evidence: This describes established molecular mechanisms of inflammation in atherosclerosis.

claim: CRP is an established biomarker of systemic inflammation and a possible predictor of future cardiovascular events.
source: Today, CRP is an established biomarker of systemic inflammation and a possible predictor of future cardiovascular events (Libby, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by the citation to Libby, 2006.

claim: Nearly 150 years ago, acute infection with Bacillus typhosus was found to cause sclerosing changes in the arterial wall.
source: Nearly 150 years ago, acute infection with Bacillus typhosus was found to cause sclerosing changes in the arterial wall (Gilbert and Lion, 1889).
evidence: This statement is supported by the citation to Gilbert and Lion, 1889.

claim: CHD-positive individuals show an increased likelihood of having elevated levels of antibodies to Chlamydia pneumoniae (C. pneumoniae).
source: A century later, the interest for a potential role of infection in atherosclerosis was renewed, with the discovery that CHD-positive individuals show an increased likelihood of having elevated levels of antibodies to Chlamydia pneumoniae (C. pneumoniae) (Saikku et al., 1988).
evidence: This statement is supported by the citation to Saikku et al., 1988.

claim: Several infectious agents, including Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori), hepatitis C virus (HCV), and human herpes viruses, have been associated with CHD.
source: This was followed by the discovery of the association with CHD of several other infectious agents, including bacteria and viruses, such as Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori), hepatitis C virus (HCV), and human herpes viruses (Adinolfi et al., 2018; Filardo et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: One proposed mechanism linking infection to atherosclerosis involves the production of pro-inflammatory molecules in response to an infection.
source: One proposed mechanism involves the production of pro-inflammatory molecules in response to an infection (Campbell and Rosenfeld, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by the citation to Campbell and Rosenfeld, 2015.

claim: Pro-inflammatory molecules such as cytokines can increase the activity of cells involved in atherosclerosis, such as macrophages and smooth muscle cells, leading to the formation of plaques.
source: These molecules, such as cytokines, can increase the activity of cells involved in atherosclerosis, such as macrophages and smooth muscle cells, leading to the formation of plaques and other changes in the walls of arteries (Campbell and Rosenfeld, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by the citation to Campbell and Rosenfeld, 2015.

claim: Another mechanism linking infection to atherosclerosis is characterized by the presence of infectious agents within the atherosclerotic plaques.
source: Another mechanism is related to the inflammation at the site of vessel wall. Specifically, it is characterized by the presence of the infectious agents within the atherosclerotic plaques.
evidence: This describes a proposed mechanism based on the presence of pathogens in plaques.

claim: The infectious consequences on the atherosclerotic plaque can be accelerated progression or a final complication like thrombosis and plaque rupture.
source: The infectious consequences on the atherosclerotic plaque can be accelerated progression or a final complication like thrombosis and plaque rupture (Pedicino et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by the citation to Pedicino et al., 2013.

claim: During the follow-up of 4500 days (12.3 years), at least one CHD event occurred in 210 individuals (6.07%).
source: During the follow-up of 4500 days (12.3 years), at least one CHD event occurred in 210 individuals (6.07%).
evidence: This is a direct report of the observed CHD incidence in the study cohort.

claim: The number of participants with one, two, and three coronary events was 140, 47, and 14, respectively.
source: The number of participants with one, two, and three coronary events was 140, 47, and 14, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct report of the distribution of CHD events in the study cohort.

claim: Nine individuals had between four and eight coronary events.
source: Nine individuals had between four and eight coronary events.
evidence: This is a direct report of the number of individuals with multiple CHD events.

claim: Eligible study participants were on average 52.8 (standard deviation [SD] ± 10.5) years of age at baseline.
source: Eligible study participants were on average 52.8 (standard deviation [SD] ± 10.5) years of age at baseline, 54% were women and 25.5% were smokers.
evidence: This is a direct report of baseline demographic characteristics of the study cohort.

claim: 54% of eligible study participants were women.
source: Eligible study participants were on average 52.8 (standard deviation [SD] ± 10.5) years of age at baseline, 54% were women and 25.5% were smokers.
evidence: This is a direct report of baseline demographic characteristics of the study cohort.

claim: 25.5% of eligible study participants were smokers.
source: Eligible study participants were on average 52.8 (standard deviation [SD] ± 10.5) years of age at baseline, 54% were women and 25.5% were smokers.
evidence: This is a direct report of baseline demographic characteristics of the study cohort.

claim: The average body mass index (BMI) of study participants was 25.5 (±4.3) kg/m2.
source: On average, their body mass index (BMI) was 25.5 (±4.3) kg/m2, their systolic blood pressure was 129 (±18) mmHg, and their HDL cholesterol level was 1.66 (±0.43) mmol/L.
evidence: This is a direct report of baseline clinical characteristics of the study cohort.

claim: The average systolic blood pressure of study participants was 129 (±18) mmHg.
source: On average, their body mass index (BMI) was 25.5 (±4.3) kg/m2, their systolic blood pressure was 129 (±18) mmHg, and their HDL cholesterol level was 1.66 (±0.43) mmol/L.
evidence: This is a direct report of baseline clinical characteristics of the study cohort.

claim: The average HDL cholesterol level of study participants was 1.66 (±0.43) mmol/L.
source: On average, their body mass index (BMI) was 25.5 (±4.3) kg/m2, their systolic blood pressure was 129 (±18) mmHg, and their HDL cholesterol level was 1.66 (±0.43) mmol/L.
evidence: This is a direct report of baseline clinical characteristics of the study cohort.

claim: The overall seropositivity for the 22 pathogens tested ranged from 3.99% (S. gallolyticus) to 96.80% (EBV).
source: The overall seropositivity ranged from 3.99% (S. gallolyticus) to 96.80% (EBV).
evidence: This is a direct report of the serological findings in the study cohort.

claim: Rubella, C. tetani and C. diphteriae were excluded from further analyses as the antibodies detected against these pathogens were most likely induced by vaccination.
source: Rubella, C. tetani and C. diphteriae were excluded from further analyses as the antibodies detected against these pathogens were most likely induced by vaccination.
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on the inference that antibodies to these pathogens are vaccine-induced.

claim: SCORE2 was significantly and positively associated with CHD (HR 1.72, 95% CI 1.61–1.85, p = 2.87×10−61).
source: To validate the utility of SCORE2 in our cohort, we tested its association with CHD. SCORE2 was significantly and positively associated with CHD (HR 1.72, 95% CI 1.61–1.85, p = 2.87×10−61) (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the univariable Cox regression analysis performed in the study.

claim: There is a significant inverse association between average gross monthly income and CHD risk (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.76–0.96, p = 7.27×10−3).
source: We also observed a significant inverse association between average gross monthly income and CHD risk (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.76–0.96, p = 7.27×10−3).
evidence: This is a finding from the univariable Cox regression analysis performed in the study.

claim: HSV-1 seropositivity is significantly positively associated with CHD (HR 1.88, 95% CI 1.30–2.68, p = 6.52×10−4).
source: We found significant positive associations for six of them, including three herpes viruses, namely HSV-1 (HR 1.88, 95% CI 1.30–2.68, p = 6.52×10−4), HHV-6A (HR 1.39, 95% CI 1.03–1.86, p = 2.89×10−2), and VZV (HR 1.70, 95% CI 1.02–2.82, p = 4.25×10−2), one polyomavirus, HPyV6 (HR 1.66, 95% CI 1.06–2.61, p = 2.74×10−2), and two bacteria, F. nucleatum (HR 1.66, 95% CI 1.20–2.29, p = 2.32×10−3), and C. trachomatis (HR 1.45, 95% CI 1.11–1.91, p = 7.22×10−3) (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the univariable Cox regression analysis performed in the study.

claim: HHV-6A seropositivity is significantly positively associated with CHD (HR 1.39, 95% CI 1.03–1.86, p = 2.89×10−2).
source: We found significant positive associations for six of them, including three herpes viruses, namely HSV-1 (HR 1.88, 95% CI 1.30–2.68, p = 6.52×10−4), HHV-6A (HR 1.39, 95% CI 1.03–1.86, p = 2.89×10−2), and VZV (HR 1.70, 95% CI 1.02–2.82, p = 4.25×10−2), one polyomavirus, HPyV6 (HR 1.66, 95% CI 1.06–2.61, p = 2.74×10−2), and two bacteria, F. nucleatum (HR 1.66, 95% CI 1.20–2.29, p = 2.32×10−3), and C. trachomatis (HR 1.45, 95% CI 1.11–1.91, p = 7.22×10−3) (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the univariable Cox regression analysis performed in the study.

claim: VZV seropositivity is significantly positively associated with CHD (HR 1.70, 95% CI 1.02–2.82, p = 4.25×10−2).
source: We found significant positive associations for six of them, including three herpes viruses, namely HSV-1 (HR 1.88, 95% CI 1.30–2.68, p = 6.52×10−4), HHV-6A (HR 1.39, 95% CI 1.03–1.86, p = 2.89×10−2), and VZV (HR 1.70, 95% CI 1.02–2.82, p = 4.25×10−2), one polyomavirus, HPyV6 (HR 1.66, 95% CI 1.06–2.61, p = 2.74×10−2), and two bacteria, F. nucleatum (HR 1.66, 95% CI 1.20–2.29, p = 2.32×10−3), and C. trachomatis (HR 1.45, 95% CI 1.11–1.91, p = 7.22×10−3) (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the univariable Cox regression analysis performed in the study.

claim: HPyV6 seropositivity is significantly positively associated with CHD (HR 1.66, 95% CI 1.06–2.61, p = 2.74×10−2).
source: We found significant positive associations for six of them, including three herpes viruses, namely HSV-1 (HR 1.88, 95% CI 1.30–2.68, p = 6.52×10−4), HHV-6A (HR 1.39, 95% CI 1.03–1.86, p = 2.89×10−2), and VZV (HR 1.70, 95% CI 1.02–2.82, p = 4.25×10−2), one polyomavirus, HPyV6 (HR 1.66, 95% CI 1.06–2.61, p = 2.74×10−2), and two bacteria, F. nucleatum (HR 1.66, 95% CI 1.20–2.29, p = 2.32×10−3), and C. trachomatis (HR 1.45, 95% CI 1.11–1.91, p = 7.22×10−3) (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the univariable Cox regression analysis performed in the study.

claim: F. nucleatum seropositivity is significantly positively associated with CHD (HR 1.66, 95% CI 1.20–2.29, p = 2.32×10−3).
source: We found significant positive associations for six of them, including three herpes viruses, namely HSV-1 (HR 1.88, 95% CI 1.30–2.68, p = 6.52×10−4), HHV-6A (HR 1.39, 95% CI 1.03–1.86, p = 2.89×10−2), and VZV (HR 1.70, 95% CI 1.02–2.82, p = 4.25×10−2), one polyomavirus, HPyV6 (HR 1.66, 95% CI 1.06–2.61, p = 2.74×10−2), and two bacteria, F. nucleatum (HR 1.66, 95% CI 1.20–2.29, p = 2.32×10−3), and C. trachomatis (HR 1.45, 95% CI 1.11–1.91, p = 7.22×10−3) (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the univariable Cox regression analysis performed in the study.

claim: C. trachomatis seropositivity is significantly positively associated with CHD (HR 1.45, 95% CI 1.11–1.91, p = 7.22×10−3).
source: We found significant positive associations for six of them, including three herpes viruses, namely HSV-1 (HR 1.88, 95% CI 1.30–2.68, p = 6.52×10−4), HHV-6A (HR 1.39, 95% CI 1.03–1.86, p = 2.89×10−2), and VZV (HR 1.70, 95% CI 1.02–2.82, p = 4.25×10−2), one polyomavirus, HPyV6 (HR 1.66, 95% CI 1.06–2.61, p = 2.74×10−2), and two bacteria, F. nucleatum (HR 1.66, 95% CI 1.20–2.29, p = 2.32×10−3), and C. trachomatis (HR 1.45, 95% CI 1.11–1.91, p = 7.22×10−3) (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the univariable Cox regression analysis performed in the study.

claim: There is a positive relationship between individuals' hs-CRP levels and increased risk of CHD event (HR 1.91, 95% CI 1.42–2.55, p = 1.51×10−5).
source: We observed a positive relationship between individuals' hs-CRP (HR 1.91, 95% CI 1.42–2.55, p = 1.51×10−5) and TNF-α (HR 1.43, 95% CI 1.05–1.96, p = 2.46×10−2) levels, and increased risk of CHD event (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the univariable Cox regression analysis performed in the study.

claim: There is a positive relationship between individuals' TNF-α levels and increased risk of CHD event (HR 1.43, 95% CI 1.05–1.96, p = 2.46×10−2).
source: We observed a positive relationship between individuals' hs-CRP (HR 1.91, 95% CI 1.42–2.55, p = 1.51×10−5) and TNF-α (HR 1.43, 95% CI 1.05–1.96, p = 2.46×10−2) levels, and increased risk of CHD event (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the univariable Cox regression analysis performed in the study.

claim: There is a significant association between the CHD-PRS and CHD (HR 1.32, 95% CI 1.16–1.51, p = 4.29×10−5).
source: As expected, we observed a significant association between the PRS and CHD (HR 1.32, 95% CI 1.16–1.51, p = 4.29×10−5), confirming that genetic predisposition to CHD can be captured through CHD-PRS.
evidence: This is a finding from the univariable Cox regression analysis performed in the study.

claim: Genetic predisposition to CHD can be captured through CHD-PRS.
source: As expected, we observed a significant association between the PRS and CHD (HR 1.32, 95% CI 1.16–1.51, p = 4.29×10−5), confirming that genetic predisposition to CHD can be captured through CHD-PRS.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed association between CHD-PRS and CHD.

claim: The top three genetic principal components (PC1, PC2, and PC3) were not significantly associated with CHD.
source: The top three genetic principal components (PC1, PC2, and PC3) were not significantly associated with CHD (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the univariable Cox regression analysis performed in the study.

claim: No strong correlations exist between significant variables identified in univariable analyses.
source: We calculated pairwise correlations between all variables that were found to be significant in univariable analyses. Appendix 2—figure 1 and Appendix 2—figure 2 illustrate that no strong correlations exist between significant variables.
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis performed in the study.

claim: The strongest correlation was observed between SCORE2 and hs-CRP, with a Pearson's coefficient of 0.22.
source: The strongest correlation was observed between SCORE2 and hs-CRP, and between seropositivity to C. trachomatis and gross monthly household income, with Pearson's and Cramer's V coefficients of 0.22 and 0.15, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis performed in the study.

claim: The strongest correlation was observed between seropositivity to C. trachomatis and gross monthly household income, with a Cramer's V coefficient of 0.15.
source: The strongest correlation was observed between SCORE2 and hs-CRP, and between seropositivity to C. trachomatis and gross monthly household income, with Pearson's and Cramer's V coefficients of 0.22 and 0.15, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis performed in the study.

claim: All significant variables satisfied the proportional hazards assumption.
source: The proportionality assumption was tested for all significant variables using the Schoenfeld residuals. The residual tests indicated that all variables satisfied the proportional hazards assumption, revealing that the effect of all covariates are constant in time (Appendix 2—figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the proportional hazards assumption testing performed in the study.

claim: No variance inflation factor (VIF) value was indicative of co-linearity.
source: Finally, we also assessed potential co-linearity issues among predictors that could affect model fitting. No variance inflation factor (VIF) value was indicative of co-linearity.
evidence: This is a finding from the co-linearity assessment performed in the study.

claim: SCORE2 is an independent prognostic factor of CHD (HR 1.96 per SD increase, 95% CI 1.74–2.22, p = 2.42×10−27).
source: The final multivariable analysis confirmed that SCORE2 (HR 1.96 per SD increase, 95% CI 1.74–2.22, p = 2.42×10−27) is an independent prognostic factor of CHD (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the multivariable Cox regression analysis performed in the study, also shown in Figure 2.

claim: Statin intake is independently associated with CHD (HR 2.24, 95% CI 1.50–3.35, p = 9.17×10−5).
source: We also observed significant independent associations for statin intake (HR 2.24, 95% CI 1.50–3.35, p = 9.17×10−5) and for seropositivity to F. nucleatum infection (HR 1.63, 95% CI 1.08–2.45, p = 1.99×10−2).
evidence: This is a finding from the multivariable Cox regression analysis performed in the study.

claim: Seropositivity to F. nucleatum infection is independently associated with CHD (HR 1.63, 95% CI 1.08–2.45, p = 1.99×10−2).
source: We also observed significant independent associations for statin intake (HR 2.24, 95% CI 1.50–3.35, p = 9.17×10−5) and for seropositivity to F. nucleatum infection (HR 1.63, 95% CI 1.08–2.45, p = 1.99×10−2).
evidence: This is a finding from the multivariable Cox regression analysis performed in the study.

claim: 22.4% (47/210) of individuals in the CHD group were seropositive to F. nucleatum, versus 14.6% (473/3249) in the control group (p = 0.003).
source: Comparing individuals who had a least one CHD event (CHD group) against those who had no event during the follow-up period (control group), 22.4% (47/210) of the individuals in the CHD group were seropositive to F. nucleatum, versus 14.6% (473/3249) in the control group (p = 0.003) (Figure 1, Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct comparison of F. nucleatum seropositivity between CHD cases and controls, shown in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: There is a significant association between CHD occurrence and elevated CHD-PRS with an HR of 1.31 (95% CI 1.10–1.56, p = 3.32×10−3) per SD increase.
source: Lastly, we also observed a significant association between CHD occurrence and elevated CHD-PRS with an HR of 1.31 (95% CI 1.10–1.56, p = 3.32×10−3) per SD increase.
evidence: This is a finding from the multivariable Cox regression analysis performed in the study.

claim: In the univariable Cox model, pathogen burden significantly increased the risk of CHD occurrence (HR 1.11, 95% CI 1.03–1.18, p = 3.25×10−3).
source: In the univariable Cox model, pathogen burden significantly increased the risk of CHD occurrence (HR 1.11, 95% CI 1.03–1.18, p = 3.25×10−3) (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the univariable Cox regression analysis performed in the study.

claim: After adjustment with multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression, pathogen burden did not meet the level of significance for staying in the model.
source: However, after adjustment with multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression, pathogen burden did not meet the level of significance for staying in the model.
evidence: This is a finding from the multivariable Cox regression analysis performed in the study.

claim: Chronic inflammation reflected in hs-CRP level did not appear as an independent predictor of CHD in the multivariable analyses.
source: Of note, chronic inflammation reflected in hs-CRP level did not appear as an independent predictor of CHD in our analyses, as the univariable association signal was suppressed after adjustment for SCORE2 levels.
evidence: This is a finding from the multivariable Cox regression analysis performed in the study.

claim: The univariable association signal between hs-CRP and CHD was suppressed after adjustment for SCORE2 levels.
source: Of note, chronic inflammation reflected in hs-CRP level did not appear as an independent predictor of CHD in our analyses, as the univariable association signal was suppressed after adjustment for SCORE2 levels.
evidence: This is a finding from the multivariable Cox regression analysis performed in the study.

claim: Participants with a higher CHD-PRS have a greater risk of CHD, even after adjustment for all known factors.
source: We studied the effect of human genetic determinants on CHD occurrence using PRS, and we reproduced previously observed effects: participants with a higher CHD-PRS have a greater risk of CHD, even after adjustment for all known factors (Ding et al., 2011; Kullo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the multivariable Cox regression analysis performed in the study, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The individual genetic background modulates CHD risk independently from age, sex, or co-morbidities.
source: This result confirms the existence of genetic susceptibility loci for CHD, and that the individual genetic background modulates CHD risk independently from age, sex, or co-morbidities.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed independent association between CHD-PRS and CHD after adjustment for other factors.

claim: F. nucleatum is very prevalent in humans.
